summary: Specifies protecting hosts on a switched network from rogue DHCPv6 servers by filtering DHCPv6 packets at the layer 2 device. It is similar to DHCP snooping in IPv4 networks.

eli5.summary: A guard at the door stops fake helpers from handing out wrong directions.

questions: how to block rogue dhcpv6 servers
subtitle: Layer 2 switches drop DHCPv6 server messages arriving on ports where no real server is connected.

tldr.problem: On a switched network, a rogue DHCPv6 server can answer hosts with bad configuration, and hosts cannot tell it from a legitimate one.
tldr.mechanism: A layer 2 device is configured with the ports where DHCPv6-server messages are allowed, and on every other port it parses the whole IPv6 header chain and drops packets that are, or may be hiding, DHCPv6-server messages.
tldr.outcome: It protects hosts against DHCPv6-based attacks only. It does not cover Router Advertisements or attacks on DHCPv6 servers, and works best when enabled on all switches of a layer 2 domain.

today: RFC 7610 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 199, August 2015). The metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated by another RFC.

sections.title: The Idea Behind DHCPv6-Shield
sections.content:
DHCPv6-Shield protects hosts on a switched network against rogue DHCPv6 servers. A layer 2 device filters DHCPv6 messages meant for DHCPv6 clients (called DHCPv6-server messages). The most basic rule is that these messages are discarded unless they arrive on specific ports.

The idea is the IPv6 counterpart of the widely deployed IPv4 mechanism called DHCP snooping, and is analogous to Router Advertisement Guard (RA-Guard) for rogue Router Advertisements.

The scope is narrow. DHCPv6-Shield mitigates only DHCPv6-based attacks against hosts. Other configuration messages such as ICMPv6 Router Advertisements are not addressed, and attacks against DHCPv6 servers, such as Denial of Service, are not mitigated.
sections.eli5: Like a school office that only accepts notes from the teacher's door, the switch ignores helper messages from any other door.

sections.title: Terms Borrowed from RFC 7112
sections.content:
A DHCPv6-Shield device is a layer 2 device, typically a layer 2 switch, that enforces the filtering policy.

The header terms come from RFC 7112. The IPv6 Header Chain is an initial IPv6 header, zero or more extension headers, and optionally one Upper-Layer Header. If there is no Upper-Layer Header, the Next Header value 59 ("No Next Header") ends the chain. A First Fragment is a fragment with Fragment Offset equal to 0.

A second IPv6 header, as when IPv6 is tunneled over IPv6, or an ESP header counts as an Upper-Layer Header and ends the chain.
sections.eli5: A packet is like nested envelopes. The chain is the list of envelopes you must open to find the real letter inside.

sections.title: Configuration
sections.content:
Before going into production, the administrator explicitly configures which layer 2 ports may receive DHCPv6 packets destined to DHCPv6 clients. Only ports where a DHCPv6 server or relay is to be connected should be listed.

Only those explicitly configured ports may pass DHCPv6-server messages on to clients.
sections.eli5: You tell the guard in advance which doors the real helper uses. Every other door is watched.

sections.title: The Filtering Rules
sections.content:
On ports not allowed to receive DHCPv6-server messages, an implementation applies five rules:

  • It MUST parse the entire IPv6 Header Chain, with no limit on how many bytes it inspects, because a limit could let hidden server messages through.
  • If a First Fragment does not contain the entire chain up to the Upper-Layer Header, it MUST drop the packet and ought to log it as a security fault.
  • It MUST offer a configuration knob for packets with unrecognized Next Header values, defaulting to drop. In that mode such packets MUST be dropped and ought to be logged as a security fault.
  • If the packet is identified as a DHCPv6 packet for a client, it MUST be dropped and SHOULD be logged as a security alert.
  • In all other cases it MUST pass the packet as usual.

An ESP header is treated as the last header of the chain, so ESP packets are passed on to the destination host. That host decides what to do if the packet is valid and carries a DHCPv6 message.
sections.eli5: The guard opens every envelope layer. If a letter is from a fake helper, or he cannot see inside, he throws it away. Everything else goes through.

sections.title: Limits, Fragments and Deployment
sections.content:
The rules describe ideal behavior. Devices that must limit how deep they scan on the fast path should drop packets once they give up finding a protocol header, and ideally be configurable with a list of protocol header identifiers so new transport protocols are not blocked. A device that must stop searching SHOULD be configurable to pass or drop.

A host's local switch must allow DHCPv6-server messages on its ingress port and cannot know which upstream messages are valid. So DHCPv6-Shield should be enabled on all layer 2 switches of a layer 2 domain to be effective.

If an attacker sends a fragmented DHCPv6 packet on a disallowed port, the First Fragment is dropped but the other fragments pass. The victim holds buffers for fragments that never reassemble, which could cause a Denial of Service if reassembly resource management is poor. The RFC notes this is not a new attack vector, since a forged datagram with a missing fragment does the same. Hosts that allow overlapping fragments (not compliant with RFC 5722) may still be open to DHCPv6-based attacks.
sections.eli5: Guards must be at every door in the building, or a fake helper can sneak in through an unguarded one.

sections.title: Related Protections
sections.content:
The RFC says that deploying RFC 7513 can further improve a site's security by mitigating IPv6 address spoofing attacks.

It also notes that other mechanisms exist with different deployment considerations. One example is a Secure DHCPv6 draft that authenticates DHCPv6-server packets when the servers' IPv6 addresses can be pre-configured at clients.
sections.eli5: There are other ways to spot fake helpers, such as checking their name tags, but each needs different setup.

viz.caption: THE FIVE FILTERING RULES ON NON-ALLOWED PORTS

items.label: Parse everything
items.desc: Parse the entire IPv6 Header Chain with no byte limit.

items.label: Incomplete First Fragment
items.desc: Drop it if it lacks the whole header chain.

items.label: Unknown Next Header
items.desc: Drop by default, via a configuration knob.

items.label: DHCPv6-server message
items.desc: Drop it and log a security alert.
